<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
Let $G$ be a locally compact group.
    We say that $\pi: \operatorname{C}_c({G}) \to \operatorname{C}_c({G})$ is a {\itshape spherical projector} if $\pi$ satisfies all of the following conditions.
    For convenience, we set $I(f) = \int_G f(x) \,\mathrm{d} x$ for $f \in \operatorname{C}_c({G})$.
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[(\textbf{SH}\textsubscript{1})] 
            For every $f,g \in \operatorname{C}_c({G})$,
            \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
                \item $\pi^2 = \pi$ and preserves positivity,
                \item $\pi(\pi(f) \cdot g) = \pi(f) \cdot \pi(g)$,
                \item $I(\pi(f) \cdot g) = I(f \cdot \pi(g))$, and
                \item $I(\pi(f)) = I(f)$.
            \end{enumerate}
        \item[(\textbf{SH}\textsubscript{2})] 
            For every $f,g \in \operatorname{C}_c({G})$, $\pi(\pi(f) * \pi(g)) = \pi(f) * \pi(g)$.
        \item[(\textbf{SH}\textsubscript{3})] 
            Let $\pi$ also denote the adjoint map on $\operatorname{M}(G)$, and for $x \in G$, denote $O_x = \operatorname{supp}(\pi(\delta_{x}))$.
            For every $x,y \in G$,
            \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
                \item either $O_x \cap O_y = \emptyset$ or $O_x = O_y$,
                \item if $x \in O_y$ then ${x^{-1}} \in O_{{y^{-1}}}$,
                \item if $O_{xy} = O_e$ then $O_x = O_{{y^{-1}}}$, and
                \item the mapping $x \mapsto O_x$ under the so-called ``Michael topology'' (defined in \cite[Section 2.5]{jewett}) is continuous.
            \end{enumerate}
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
As defined above, $\pi$ is a spherical projector.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Verifying that \eqref{eq:action-spherical-proj} satisfies \textbf{SH}\textsubscript{1} and \textbf{SH}\textsubscript{2} is a series of straightforward algebraic computations.
    For \textbf{SH}\textsubscript{3}, it is clear that $\operatorname{supp} \pi(\delta_x)$ is precisely the $K$-orbit of $x$, from which it immediately follows that $\pi$ satisfies (i), (ii) and (iii) of \textbf{SH}\textsubscript{3}.
    Lastly, one may check that the Michael topology, when restricted to the orbits of $K$, coincides with the usual quotient topology.
    Thus the map $x \mapsto O_x$ is continuous.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
It should be noted that the ``$K$-radial'' terminology slightly differs from the paper of Muruganandam.
    They use the term ``$\pi$-radial'' instead of $K$-radial, and opts for notation such as $\mathrm{A}_\pi(G)$.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:hyper-herz}
    Let $K$ act on a locally compact group $G$, and let $N$ be a closed $K$-invariant subgroup of $G$.
    Then
    \begin{equation*}
        {                                            
  \left.\kern-\nulldelimiterspace                                           
  \mathop{\mathrm{Z}_{K}\mathrm{A}}(G)               
  \vphantom{\big|}                                              
  \right|_{N}                        
  } = \mathop{\mathrm{Z}_{K}\mathrm{A}}(N)
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Let $\pi_G : \operatorname{A}(G) \to \operatorname{A}(G)$ and $\pi_N : \operatorname{A}(N) \to \operatorname{A}(N)$ denote the $K$-spherical projectors for $G$ and $N$ respectively, and let $R : \operatorname{A}(G) \to \operatorname{A}(N)$ denote the restriction map.

    The spherical projectors will be given by a formula as in \eqref{eq:action-spherical-proj}, though they will be defined on their respective Fourier algebras.
    It follows from this that $R \pi_G = \pi_N R$.
    Thus if $u \in \mathop{\mathrm{Z}_{K}\mathrm{A}}(G)$ and $v = Ru$, then 
    \begin{equation*}
        \pi_N v = \pi_N R u = R \pi_G u = R u = v
    \end{equation*}
    and so $Ru \in \mathop{\mathrm{Z}_{K}\mathrm{A}}(N)$.
    Surjectivity follows by Herz's restriction theorem.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:discrete-hypergroup-dirac}
    Let $K$ act on a discrete group $\Gamma$, with associated spherical projector $\pi$.
    Then $\pi(\delta_{x}) \in \mathop{\mathrm{Z}_{K}\mathrm{\ell}^1}(\Gamma)$ with
    \begin{equation*}
        \pi(\delta_{x}) = \frac{1}{\card{{K} \mathrel{{\boldsymbol{\cdot}}} {x}}} {\mathbbm{1}}_{{K} \mathrel{{\boldsymbol{\cdot}}} {x}} 
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Since ${K} \mathrel{{\boldsymbol{\cdot}}} {x}$ is finite, it follows by the orbit stabiliser theorem that $K/{K}_{x}$ is finite and hence
                       
                           
                                               
                                                                                                         
                                                                      
                     
    \begin{align*}
        \pi(f)(y)
        = \int_K f({k} \mathrel{{\boldsymbol{\cdot}}} {y}) \,\mathrm{d} k
        = \frac{1}{\card{K/{K}_{y}}} \sum_{l {K}_{y} \in K/{K}_{y}} f({l} \mathrel{{\boldsymbol{\cdot}}} {y})
        = \frac{1}{\card{{K} \mathrel{{\boldsymbol{\cdot}}} {y}}} \sum_{z \in {K} \mathrel{{\boldsymbol{\cdot}}} {y}} f(z)
    \end{align*}
    for $f \in \operatorname{\ell}^{1} 
    \def#1{\Gamma} 
    \ifx#1\empty
         
    \else
        (\Gamma) 
    \fi 
$.
    Thus we have
    \begin{equation*}
        \pi(\delta_{x})(y)
        = \frac{1}{\card{{K} \mathrel{{\boldsymbol{\cdot}}} {y}}} \sum_{z \in {K} \mathrel{{\boldsymbol{\cdot}}} {y}} \delta_{x}(z)
        = \frac{1}{\card{{K} \mathrel{{\boldsymbol{\cdot}}} {x}}} {\mathbbm{1}}_{{K} \mathrel{{\boldsymbol{\cdot}}} {x}}(y) \qedhere
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:cfalg-quot-kfalg}
    Let $G$ be an abelian compact group, and $K$ a compact group acting on $G$.
    Then
    \begin{equation*}
        {                                            
  \left.\kern-\nulldelimiterspace                                           
  \operatorname{ZA}({G \rtimes K})               
  \vphantom{\big|}                                              
  \right|_{G}                        
  } = \mathop{\mathrm{Z}_{K}\mathrm{A}}(G)
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
By \cref{thm:hyper-herz}, we have that ${                                            
  \left.\kern-\nulldelimiterspace                                           
  \operatorname{ZA}({G \rtimes K})               
  \vphantom{\big|}                                              
  \right|_{G}                        
  } = \mathop{\mathrm{Z}_{{G \rtimes K}}\mathrm{A}}(G)$.
    However, since $G$ is abelian, observe that
                       
                              
                                                       
                                 
                         
                     
    \begin{equation*}
        (gk)h(gk)^{-1}
        = g ({k} \mathrel{{\boldsymbol{\cdot}}} {h}) {g^{-1}}
        ={k} \mathrel{{\boldsymbol{\cdot}}} {h}
    \end{equation*}
    for $g,h \in G$ and $k \in K$.
    If we let $\pi_{{G \rtimes K}}$ and $\pi_K$ be the associated spherical projectors, we then have that $\pi_{{G \rtimes K}}(gk) = \pi_K(k)$, and so we obtain that $\mathop{\mathrm{Z}_{{G \rtimes K}}\mathrm{A}}(G) = \mathop{\mathrm{Z}_{K}\mathrm{A}}(G)$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
With $H$ and $\widehat{H}$ as above, the dual of $H$ is in fact $\widehat{H}$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Recall that $\operatorname{M}(\widehat{H})$ can be identified with $\mathop{\mathrm{Z}_{K}\mathrm{M}}(\widehat{G})$, and consider the Fourier-Stieltjes transform $\mathcal{F} : \operatorname{M}(\widehat{G}) \to \operatorname{C}_b({G})$.
    Bochner's Theorem and \cref{thm:mu-radial} below show that $\mathcal{F}(\operatorname{Prob}(\widehat{H})) = \operatorname{P}_1(G,K)$.
    This map preserves the extreme points and the hyperproduct (as convolutions become multiplication) so it follows that $\widehat{H}$ is isomorphic to $\operatorname{E}(G,K)$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:mu-radial}
    Given $K \curvearrowright G$, we have that $\mu \in \operatorname{M}(G)$ is $K$-radial if and only if its Fourier-Stieltjes transform $\widehat{\mu} \in \operatorname{C}_b({\widehat{G}})$ is $K$-radial.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
We let $\pi$ and $\hat{\pi}$ be the spherical projectors of $K \curvearrowright G$ and $K \curvearrowright \widehat{G}$ respectively.
    For $\mu \in \operatorname{M}(G)$, observe that
    \begin{align*}
        \hat{\pi}(\widehat{\mu})(\chi)
        &= \int_K \widehat{\mu}({k} \mathrel{{\boldsymbol{\cdot}}} {\chi}) \,\mathrm{d} k \\
        &= \int_K \int_G \overline{\dup{{k} \mathrel{{\boldsymbol{\cdot}}} {\chi}}{x}} \,\mathrm{d} \mu(x) \,\mathrm{d} k \\
        &= \int_K \int_G \overline{\dup{\chi}{{{k^{-1}}} \mathrel{{\boldsymbol{\cdot}}} {x}}} \,\mathrm{d} \mu(x) \,\mathrm{d} k
    \end{align*}
    and if we let $f_\chi(x) = \overline{\dup{\chi}{x}}$, then
    \begin{align*}
        \hat{\pi}(\widehat{\mu})(\chi)
        &= \int_G \int_K f_\chi({{k^{-1}}} \mathrel{{\boldsymbol{\cdot}}} {x}) \,\mathrm{d} k \,\mathrm{d} \mu(x) \\
        &= \int_G \pi(f_\chi)(x) \,\mathrm{d} \mu(x) \\
        &= \int_G f_\chi(x) \,\mathrm{d} \pi(\mu)(x) \\
        &= \int_G \overline{\dup{\chi}{x}} \,\mathrm{d} \pi(\mu)(x)
        = \widehat{\pi(\mu)}(\chi)
    \end{align*}
    and from this, it is clear that $\mu$ is $K$-radial if and only if $\widehat{\mu}$ is $K$-radial.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
A hypergroup $H$ satisfies the {\itshape 1-Leptin $(L_1)$} condition if for every compact $C \subseteq H$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists a measurable $V \subseteq H$ such that $0 < \mathbf{m}_H(V) < \infty$ with $\mathbf{m}_H(C*V)/\mathbf{m}_H(V) < 1 + \varepsilon$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:alaghmandan}
    Let $H$ be a discrete commutative hypergroup which satisfies $(L_1)$.
    If $\operatorname{\ell}^{1} 
    \def#1{H} 
    \ifx#1\empty
         
    \else
        (H) 
    \fi 
$ is amenable, then there is some $M \geq 1$ such that $\set{x \in H : \mathbf{m}_H(x) \leq M}$ is infinite.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\leavevmode
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
        \item Let $K$ be a compact group acting on a compact group $G$.
            We say that $K \curvearrowright G$ is {\itshape (compactly) layered by $G_n$} if $G_n$ is a decreasing chain of subgroups whose intersection is trivial, such that the orbits of $K \curvearrowright G$ are precisely the sets $A_n := G_{n} \setminus G_{n+1}$ and $\set{e}$.
        \item 
            Let $K$ be a compact group acting on a discrete group $\Gamma$.
            We say that $K \curvearrowright \Gamma$ is {\itshape (discretely) layered by $\Gamma_n$} if $\Gamma_n$ is an increasing chain of subgroups whose union is all of $\Gamma$, such that the orbits of $K \curvearrowright \Gamma$ are precisely the sets $B_n := \Gamma_{n} \setminus \Gamma_{n-1}$.
            For convenience, we assume that $\Gamma_0 = \set{e}$ and $\Gamma_{-1} = \emptyset$.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:orbits-fd}
    The orbits of the action of $\operatorname{GL}_{d}(R)$ on the vector space $F^d$ are precisely the sets $\set{0}$ and $M_d^n \setminus M_d^{n+1}$ for $n \in {\mathbb{Z}}$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
It is straightforward to see that the sets $M_d^{n}$ are invariant under the action of $K$.
    So it remains to show is that their differences are in fact full orbits.
    Without loss of generality, it suffices to prove that $M_d^0 \setminus M_d^1 = R^d\setminus M_d^1$ is an orbit.
    Set $e_1 \in R^d$ to be the usual basis element, and take $x = (x_1, \ldots, x_d) \in R^d \setminus M_d^1$.
    Since $K$ contains the permutation matrices, we may assume without loss of generality that $x_1 \in R \setminus M$.
    Now let $A \in K$ be the matrix
    \begin{equation*}
        A = \begin{bmatrix}
            x_1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
            x_2 & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\
                                        
            \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
            x_d & 0 & \cdots & 1 
        \end{bmatrix}
    \end{equation*}
    where $A$ is invertible since $x_1 \in R^*$.
    Clearly $A e_1 = x$, and so $x$ is in the orbit of $e_1$.
    By transitivity, we have that $R^d\setminus M_d^1$ is an orbit.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:dvr-dual-layering}
    $K_d \curvearrowright G_d$ is compactly layered and $K_d \curvearrowright \widehat{G_d}$ is discretely layered.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
In both cases, the layering is given as in \cref{thm:orbits-fd}.
    It suffices to observe that $R^d$ is a subgroup of $F^d$, and so the compact layering is given directly by $M_d^n$.
    For the dual version, note that the dual of $R^d$ is isomorphic to $F^d/R^d$, so the discrete layering is given by $M_d^{-n}/R^d$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:l1-dual-profinite}
    Let $H$ be the orbit hypergroup of $K \curvearrowright G$ for a locally compact group $G$.
    If $G$ is the direct limit of $K$-invariant compact open subgroups $G_n$, then $H$ satisfies $(L_1)$.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Let $C \subseteq H$ be compact, which we will consider as a $K$-invariant compact subset of $G$.
    Since the subgroups $G_n$ are open, there must be a sufficiently large $N$ such that $C \subseteq G_N$.
    We then have that $C * G_N \subseteq G_N$, and so it follows that $\mathbf{m}_H(C * G_N)/\mathbf{m}_H(G_N) \leq 1$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:layered-non-amenability}
    Let $\Gamma$ be a discrete abelian group, and suppose that $K \curvearrowright \Gamma$ is a discretely layered action.
    If we let $G = \widehat{\Gamma}$, then $\mathop{\mathrm{Z}_{K}\mathrm{A}}(G)$ is not amenable.
    In particular, $\operatorname{ZA}({G \rtimes K})$ is also not amenable.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Let $H$ denote the orbit hypergroup for $K \curvearrowright \Gamma$.
    By \cref{thm:discrete-hypergroup-dirac}, the elements of $H$ are of the form
    \begin{equation}
        b_n 
        = \frac{1}{\card{B_n}} {\mathbbm{1}}_{B_n}
        = \frac{1}{\card{\Gamma_n} - \card{\Gamma_{n-1}}} \left({\mathbbm{1}}_{\Gamma_{n}} - {\mathbbm{1}}_{\Gamma_{n-1}}\right)
    \end{equation}
    with Haar measure $\mathbf{m}_H (b_n) = \card{\Gamma_n} - \card{\Gamma_{n-1}}$.
    These clearly grow without bound, so that for any $M > 0$, the equation $\mathbf{m}_H(b_n) \geq M$ holds for all but finitely many $n$.
    Since $H$ is $(L_1)$ by \cref{thm:l1-dual-profinite}, then by \cref{thm:alaghmandan} we have that $\operatorname{L}^{1} 
    \def#1{H} 
    \ifx#1\empty
         
    \else
        (H) 
    \fi 
 = \operatorname{A}(\widehat{H}) = \mathop{\mathrm{Z}_{K}\mathrm{A}}(G)$ is not amenable.
    The final statement follows by \cref{thm:cfalg-quot-kfalg}.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
$\operatorname{ZA}({R^d \rtimes \operatorname{GL}_{d}(R)})$ is not amenable.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- conjecture-1: body_md -->
\label{cnj:layer-to-dual}
    Let $G$ be a compact abelian group, and let $K$ be a compact group acting on $G$.
    If $K \curvearrowright G$ is compactly layered by $G_n$, then $K \curvearrowright \widehat{G}$ is discretely layered by $F_n = {G_n}^\perp$.
<!-- end conjecture-1 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Without loss of generality, it suffices to show that $F_1 \setminus \set{e}$ is an orbit.
    To this end, consider the natural action of $K$ on the quotient $G/G_1$.
    By assumption this has two orbits: the trivial orbit and everything else.
    Let us say that such actions are {\itshape transitive}.

    Notice that $G/G_1$ is finite.
    So by transitivity, every (non-trivial) element must have the same order, and hence it is of the form $\mathbb{F}_{q}^n$ where $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ is the finite field of order $q$.
    We also have that $F_1 \cong \widehat{G/G_1} \cong \widehat{\mathbb{F}_{q}^n} \cong \mathbb{F}_{q}^n$.
    All that remains now is to show that $K \curvearrowright F_1$ is also transitive.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- conjecture-2: body_md -->
Let $G$ be a transitive subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q})$ acting on $\mathbb{F}_{q}^n$.
    Then the transpose group $G^T$ is also transitive on $\mathbb{F}_{q}^n$.
<!-- end conjecture-2 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:hyp-comb}
    Let $H$ be a discrete layered hypergroup coming from the action $K \curvearrowright \Gamma$, and assume the notation as given above.
    For $n > m \geq 0$ we have
    \begin{equation*}
        b_n * b_m = b_n
        \qquad \text{and} \qquad
        b_n * b_n = \frac{1}{q_n - q_{n-1}}\left[\sum_{i=0}^{n} (q_{i} - q_{i-1})b_i - q_{n-1}b_n\right]
    \end{equation*}
    where we set $q_{-1} := 0$ for convenience.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The definition of convolution immediately yields that $g_n * g_m (x) = \card{\Gamma_n \cap x \Gamma_m}$, and so $g_n * g_m = g_m * g_n = g_m$ for $m \leq n$.
    Supposing now that $m < n$, we have
    \begin{align*}
        b_n * b_m
        &= \frac{(g_n - g_{n-1})*(g_m - g_{m-1})}{(q_n - q_{n-1})(q_m - q_{m-1})} \\
        &= \frac{q_m g_n - q_{m-1} g_n - q_m g_{n-1} + q_{m-1}g_{n-1}}{(q_n - q_{n-1})(q_m - q_{m-1})} \\
        &= \frac{(q_m - q_{m-1}) (g_n - g_{n-1})}{(q_n - q_{n-1})(q_m - q_{m-1})}  = b_n
    \end{align*}
    Similarly, we can compute 
    \begin{align*}
        b_n * b_n
        &= \frac{(g_n - g_{n-1})*(g_n - g_{n-1})}{(q_n - q_{n-1})^2} \\
        &= \frac{q_n g_n - 2 q_{n-1} g_n + q_{n-1}g_{n-1}}{(q_n - q_{n-1})^2}\\
        &= \frac{(q_n - q_{n-1}) g_n - q_{n-1} (g_n - g_{n-1})}{(q_n - q_{n-1})^2}\\
        &= \frac{g_n - q_{n-1} b_n}{q_n - q_{n-1}}
    \end{align*}
    Since $b_n$ is a weighted difference of $g_n$ and $g_{n-1}$, we can reverse this to obtain $g_n = \sum_{i=0}^{n} (q_{i} - q_{i-1})b_i$, from which it follows that
    \begin{equation*}
        b_n * b_n = \frac{1}{q_n - q_{n-1}}\left[\sum_{i=0}^{n} (q_{i} - q_{i-1})b_i - q_{n-1}b_n\right]\qedhere
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end proof-12 -->
